clue.text: Accompanied by star, left behind with knowledge of Glasgow sports venue

parts.note: Scots — a Glaswegian's 'kenning' is knowledge, as in 'beyond my kennin'
as in singing to a piano — 'to' an accompaniment
an exploding star
L = left; 'behind' puts the whole TO-NOVA-L run after KENNING

explanation.walkthrough: Don't hunt for a Glasgow ground: the Oval is in London, and 'Glasgow' is only there to flag KENNING as Scots for knowledge. 'Behind' tells you the star-and-left assembly follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: This south London ground is the home of Surrey County Cricket Club and a Test match venue, so a sports venue by any measure.

clue.text: Charles and his mum in dust-up about constant sleazy activity

parts.note: King Charles — K…ING wraps round everything else
Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen's royal cypher
split round the constant
c — the speed of light, physics' favourite constant

explanation.walkthrough: Two containers at once: KING (Charles) wraps everything, and inside it the BRAWL wraps the C. ER = Elizabeth Regina is a convention worth learning — setters lean on royal cyphers constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: Driving slowly along the roadside to solicit prostitutes is a seedy, often illegal practice, so the phrase names a sleazy activity outright.

clue.text: Water nymph transformed by Diana

parts.note: the goddess supplies her own five letters

explanation.walkthrough: Diana's own letters rearrange into one of the nymphs who attended the goddess of the hunt — surface and wordplay are the same five letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth these spirits presided over springs, rivers and fountains, so the term names a freshwater nymph precisely.

clue.text: Mostly where soldiers are trained to place their trust

definitions.meaning: the everyday adverbial sense: broadly speaking, without accounting for exceptions

definitions.text: where soldiers are trained to place their trust
definitions.meaning: whimsically, troops put their faith in (their) general

explanation.walkthrough: One word of definition, then the joke: soldiers are drilled to place their trust in their general.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an everyday idiom for 'usually' or 'on the whole', while the second reading puns on troops' faith in their commanding officer.

clue.text: Harsh and unscrupulous activity, seizing racy tapes

definitions.note: the answer is used attributively, as in gestapo tactics, so it stands for an adjective here

indicators.note: the word for activity grabs hold of the shuffled letters, so they sit inside it

parts.note: go means energy or activity, as in 'full of go'

indicators.note: racy means lively and spirited, so the letters of tapes are set jumping into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone condemns a ruthless operation that confiscates a stash of risqué videotapes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Racy tapes' reads as one phrase, but racy is the anagram signal working on tapes alone.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nazi secret police gave its name to any brutal, ruthless methods, so the word describes tactics that are cruel and unprincipled.

clue.text: Awfully sick after leaving new soup kitchen, getting better

indicators.note: awfully suggests something done badly, so the letters that remain are scrambled into a new order
once the letters of sick have departed, what remains of the longer phrase is what gets rearranged

explanation.surface: A charity kitchen serving soup, once the sick have gone, is on the mend.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the letters of sick out of soup kitchen and rearrange the seven left over; new only dresses the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To be on the up is an idiom for improving or rising in fortune, so it matches getting better.

clue.text: Start rolling the cameras here

definitions.meaning: the straight dictionary sense: a noun for the beginning of something
split into two words, this names the location on a film shoot where the cameras roll

explanation.walkthrough: A start, or where filming starts: on set. The second reading is the whimsical one, which is why it carries the cameras.
explanation.definitionFit: As one word it is a plain synonym for a beginning; split in two it names the film studio floor where shooting happens.

clue.text: Notices surrounding hip-hop doctor's name on envelope

parts.note: the first of the two 'notices' — a small ad
Dr Dre's — sandwiched by the notices

explanation.walkthrough: 'Notices' is plural for a reason: the one word supplies two separate pieces, one at each end of the answer. Spotting that a single word does double duty is the step most solvers miss.
explanation.definitionFit: The recipient of a letter is the person whose name is written on the front of the envelope, so the definition describes them by that label.

clue.text: Regretful of £1000 deposited after bankruptcy

definitions.note: 'Ruing' is a participle and 'regretful of' an adjective phrase, but they swap cleanly — 'ruing the loss' means 'regretful of the loss' — so the definition is fair.

parts.note: financial ruin
a grand — standard crossword currency

explanation.walkthrough: G for grand — £1000 — is a staple abbreviation; 'deposited after' banks it at the end of the ruin.
explanation.definitionFit: To rue something is to feel sorrow or remorse over it, so the participle matches being regretful of a thing.

clue.text: Discarded top class team

parts.note: school streaming: the top class is Set A
a side, as in a football side

explanation.walkthrough: School streaming does the work — in many schools the top class is called Set A, and a side is a team in sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Something put aside has been rejected or dropped for now, as when a court annuls a verdict, a close synonym for thrown out.

clue.text: Sorcerer welcomes assistance getting diplomat initial crossing?

parts.note: M…AGE, wrapped round the rest
help
an envoy

explanation.walkthrough: The sorcerer swallows both the help and the diplomat. 'Initial crossing' is the definition — a ship's first trip across the water.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel's first ever passage, like the Titanic's ill-fated Atlantic run; the question mark admits the definition works by description.

clue.text: Solo turn by crossword guru touring centre of 1ac?

parts.note: Jonathan Crowther — Azed of the Observer, the setters' setter
the middle letter of ONE, which Azed 'tours' (wraps round): AZ-N-ED
the 'ac' tags along as letters; then the whole AZNED-AC does a turn

explanation.walkthrough: Azed took his pseudonym from Deza, a Spanish Grand Inquisitor, spelt backwards — so sending him round a turn is a fitting tribute. The question mark owns up to the liberties taken with '1ac'.
explanation.definitionFit: In a concerto this is the virtuoso passage where the orchestra falls silent and the soloist plays alone, so a solo by definition.

clue.text: Maximum and minimum values taken out of context, remarkably

parts.note: spelled out across the two words: contEXT REMArkably

explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken out of context' sounds like a complaint about quotation, but it is a literal instruction — the answer sits inside those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A mathematical term: the Latin plural for the greatest and least points a function reaches, covering maxima and minima together.

clue.text: Change location of union meeting in telephone call?

parts.note: the union is a wedding, and the altar is where it happens

explanation.walkthrough: Weddings are the 'union' here, and 'in telephone call' tells you to listen rather than read: altar and alter sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: to modify or make different, as in tailoring a suit or revising a plan.

clue.text: Actor suggesting a spot of 1dn?

parts.note: 'tom' is old slang for a prostitute — the one being crawled towards
and the same cross-reference again for the verb: to cruise is to drive slowly around looking for custom

explanation.walkthrough: The actor's name reads as a little kerb crawling: a tom on the cruise. The cross-reference to 1 down is the whole engine of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The star of Top Gun and the Mission: Impossible films is one of Hollywood's best-known leading men, so 'Actor' defines him by example.

clue.text: Under a great burden, Ms Viner perhaps, with work

parts.note: op. — an opus; 'with' bolts it on at the front
Katharine Viner edits the Guardian: a press ed.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' concedes Ms Viner is only one example of a press ed. — any newspaper editor would do.
explanation.definitionFit: People weighed down by harsh rule or heavy hardship are crushed under it, so the adjective fits someone bearing a great burden.

clue.text: Sort of alpine act a daring climb?

parts.note: nine letters to shuffle

explanation.walkthrough: El Capitan in Yosemite is the daring climb — famously scaled without ropes in Free Solo. 'Sort of' quietly does the shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: The granite monolith in California's Yosemite Valley is a famous big-wall ascent; the question mark flags that a mountain stands in for the climb itself.

clue.text: An essential for burner of midnight oil hit spot

definitions.text: An essential for burner of midnight oil

parts.note: to lam = to hit, as in 'lam into'
a spot — the tight kind

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are rougher than they look: to LAM is to hit, and the spot here is a PLIGHT. Burn the midnight oil and this is what you read by.
explanation.definitionFit: Burning the midnight oil means studying late, originally by an oil lamp, so the glow of one is what such a night owl needs.

clue.text: It's a bit gluey getting up on a cycle

parts.note: elating = uplifting, getting your spirits up

explanation.walkthrough: A rare device: 'on a cycle' means the letters rotate — push the G of ELATING from the back round to the front. Gelatin genuinely is the gluey bit: glue is made from it.
explanation.definitionFit: Boiled from animal collagen, this protein is the sticky basis of jellies and of animal glue, hence a gluey substance.

clue.text: Old drunkard beats wino up

parts.note: beats = TOPS, also sent climbing
a wino is a SOT, sent climbing

explanation.walkthrough: This is a down entry, so 'up' sends TOPS and SOT bottom-to-top together. 'Old' flags that tosspot is an archaic word for a drunkard.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally one who tosses back his pot of ale, an archaic term for a habitual boozer, which is why 'Old' qualifies the definition.

clue.text: Guiltless about Jack Sprat's diet, it's implied

parts.note: c = circa, about
he could eat no fat — so what he did eat, by implication, was the lean

explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme is the key: Jack Sprat could eat no fat, so his diet — never stated outright — was the lean.
explanation.definitionFit: Being free of wrongdoing, as in a clean record or coming clean, is an idiomatic sense matching innocent.

clue.text: Arctic resident worked in retirement with supercomputer

parts.note: HAL 9000, the computer in 2001: A Space Odyssey
w = with
worked = RAN, sent backwards 'in retirement'

explanation.walkthrough: The tusked whale of the Arctic. HAL is cinema's most famous computer, and 'in retirement' — withdrawing — is a direction-neutral way to reverse RAN.
explanation.definitionFit: This tusked whale lives year-round in Arctic waters around Greenland and Canada, so it is a polar inhabitant by example.

clue.text: Spurs are improving, reportedly (still in need of work)

definitions.note: a verb here: to heel a horse is to urge it on with the heels, and to heel a gamecock is to fit it with spurs

indicators.note: reportedly means we hear the word rather than see it, so it is a sound-alike

parts.note: heal means get better, as wounds are said to do

indicators.note: still needing, that is lacking, the word for work, so it is taken away

parts.note: to till is to work the land

explanation.surface: A jibe that Tottenham Hotspur, the London football club, are getting better but still have work to do.
explanation.walkthrough: Spurs is the nickname of the London club Tottenham Hotspur, which pulls the reader towards football; here it is a verb. The parenthesis is wordplay too, giving the final S.
explanation.definitionFit: To heel is to drive a horse forward with the heels, just as a rider urges it on with spurs.

clue.text: Cheese production initially stops its run

parts.note: 'it' = SA (sex appeal, the 'It' in It girl); the plural gives a pair of them
just its first letter, which 'stops' — plugs — the gap
a run at something = a go at it

explanation.walkthrough: Sapsago is a hard green Swiss cheese. 'It' = SA is vintage crosswordese for sex appeal; Enigmatist pluralises it to get two, then the P stops the gap between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A hard, green Swiss variety flavoured with blue fenugreek and usually grated, so the general word cheese defines it by example.

clue.text: Friend is one shot

parts.note: first person: is = am
the Roman numeral
have a shot = have a go

explanation.walkthrough: Read it as a tiny sentence: is = AM, one = I, shot = GO — and a Spanish friend appears.
explanation.definitionFit: Borrowed from Spanish, the word is used in English as a warm, informal term for a pal or companion.

clue.text: Dodge section that is recording

parts.note: s. — as in a legal citation
id est — 'that is' before it was abbreviated to i.e.
an extended-play record

explanation.walkthrough: The trick is 'that is' expanded to its full Latin, id est, rather than the usual two-letter i.e.
explanation.definitionFit: To avoid a tackle or a question by stepping out of its way is a plain verb synonym for evading it.

clue.text: Forest dweller there — fearfully symmetrical, according to recital

parts.note: Blake's 'Tyger Tyger, burning bright… thy fearful symmetry' points at the tiger, whose homophone doubles as the word for the great northern forest it prowls

explanation.walkthrough: The taiga is the great northern forest, and its most famous dweller arrives via Blake's poem — 'fearful symmetry' is the Tyger's own phrase, delivered 'according to recital'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Russian word names the vast subarctic belt of coniferous woodland across Siberia and Canada, the world's largest land biome.

clue.text: Planet's reporter takes chorus on leave, on the way to the Proms?

indicators.note: the reporter takes in the singing word, so it ends up inside his name

parts.note: Clark Kent, Superman's alter ego, is a reporter on the Daily Planet
to chorus is to sing together
taken as written
to leave is to go
re means on or about, as in a letter heading

explanation.surface: A newspaper journalist joins a choir while on holiday, heading to the summer concerts.
explanation.walkthrough: KENSINGTON GORE is the London street on which the Royal Albert Hall stands, home of the BBC Proms concert season.
explanation.definitionFit: The road runs past the Royal Albert Hall, the venue for the Proms, so it is a route to those concerts.
